beats.beat: Judith and Mr Rowe call at Oakmere under pretence of parish almsgiving, and are received stiffly by Hartwell in the hall.
Alone with Whitlow in the kitchen, Judith learns the housekeeper was told exactly what account to give of the day of the signing.
Whitlow admits, her voice dropping, that months before the death she wrote herself to Farr's regiment warning that his great-uncle was failing.
She recalls handing that letter to Hartwell to go with the rest of the post, since he had by then taken charge of it.
Frightened at having said so much, Whitlow cannot say whether the letter was ever sent at all.

turn.note: The chapter ends on genuine uncertainty about the letter's fate, which drives the search that occupies the following chapters.

problems: "which is a thing that keeps a frightened woman standing for only about a minute" is narratorial editorializing about human behaviour in general rather than a specific observation of Whitlow.
"He looked at the alms book for rather longer than a man looks at a thing he means to read" tells the reader Hartwell is suspicious rather than showing it through a concrete action.

generic_prose.quote: which is a thing that keeps a frightened woman standing for only about a minute
generic_prose.replace_with: Show Whitlow's posture change concretely — she sits, or her hand stops working the pan — rather than a generalized claim about frightened women.

generic_prose.quote: He looked at the alms book for rather longer than a man looks at a thing he means to read
generic_prose.replace_with: Give Hartwell a specific tell — turning it over, checking the date, glancing at the door — instead of a comparative generalization.

trope_note: Advances the disputed inheritance directly through Whitlow's testimony; the returning officer and forced proximity tropes sit outside this chapter's scope, which is acceptable since Farr does not appear.
length_note: Counted roughly 722 words against a 560 target, about 29% over; the overage comes from Rowe's nervous almsgiving rationale and scene-setting rather than padding, so it reads as generous coverage rather than a skipped beat.
fixes: Trim Rowe's opening almsgiving speech and the narrator's alms-book paragraph by a third; the point (a pretext, and Rowe's discomfort with it) lands in fewer words.
Replace "which is a thing that keeps a frightened woman standing for only about a minute" with a physical beat specific to Whitlow.
Replace "He looked at the alms book for rather longer than a man looks at a thing he means to read" with a concrete, visible action.
Consider cutting one of the three 'never' clauses in Whitlow's final speech ("I never saw it after. I never saw it in the bag and I never saw it burnt") to avoid the rule-of-three cadence.
